Q: Creating a tibble with specific information pulled out A:

You can use a tsibble, a data infrastructure for tidy temporal data

library(tsibble)
library(lubridate)

as_tsibble(co2) |> 
  mutate(year = year(index), date = ym(index))
# A tsibble: 468 x 4 [1M]
      index value  year date
      <mth> <dbl> <dbl> <date>
 1 1959 Jan  315.  1959 1959-01-01
 2 1959 Feb  316.  1959 1959-02-01
 3 1959 Mar  316.  1959 1959-03-01
 4 1959 Apr  318.  1959 1959-04-01
 5 1959 May  318.  1959 1959-05-01
 6 1959 Jun  318   1959 1959-06-01
 7 1959 Jul  316.  1959 1959-07-01
 8 1959 Aug  315.  1959 1959-08-01
 9 1959 Sep  314.  1959 1959-09-01
10 1959 Oct  313.  1959 1959-10-01
# ℹ 458 more rows

Q: Get Start date of a current partnership A:

The important thing is to add a 'partnership number' for every male ID that will group multiple records together. The following query should get you started:

Select p.*,sum(changeover) Over (Partition by MaleID Order by Ball_Start Rows Between Unbounded Preceding and Current Row) as PartnerID
FROM (
    Select p1.*,Case When FemaleID=Lag(FemaleID) Over (Partition By MaleID Order By Ball_Start) Then 0 Else 1 End as changeover
    From tblPartnerships p1
) p

You can reference the result of this query to save only the latest (maximum) partnerid, and group by it as well to find min(dates). But the partnerID is the important part.

This was coded as a nested query because most DBMS don't allow multiple window functions in an expression.

Q: NestJS clean architecture repository pattern A:

When using MongoDB with clean architecture:

  • Schema (Infrastructure): Defines DB structure (e.g., via Mongoose).

  • Repository (Data layer): Wraps DB operations (CRUD), hides MongoDB details.

  • Interface (Contract): Defines repository methods (used by service, not implementation).

  • Service (Application): Contains business logic and calls repository (never MongoDB directly).

Flow:

Controller → Service → Repository → Schema → MongoDB

Key rule: Service depends on interface, not MongoDB → keeps code testable and DB-independent.

Q: How do I copy files to a volume when composing? A:

A container is a wrapper around a process. Your "frontend" and "backend" containers make sense because the process in each of those is an HTTP server. A standalone directory of Typescript types does not make sense because it doesn't run a process, it's just a collection of source files.

There's one more conceptual issue with the setup you propose. Volume mounts happen only after an image is built, when a container is created. However, you're going to need the types directory to build the image. A volume mount won't help you here.

To use this shared directory, you're going to need a setup as is described in How to include files outside of Docker's build context?. At a Compose level it would look roughly like

services:
  frontend:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: frontend/Dockerfile  # (conventionally with a capital "D")
    # and no volumes:

In the frontend/Dockerfile, when you COPY files into your image, you need to make sure the paths on the left-hand side are relative to the top of the source tree.

FROM node
WORKDIR /app
COPY frontend/ frontend/
COPY types/ types/
WORKDIR /app/frontend
RUN npm ci
...

(I have a strong opinion that you should try very hard to avoid using volumes: to inject code into a container. Standard Docker deployment patterns do not check out the source code on the host system, it should be fully built into the image. If you're overwriting the image's code with whatever exists on the local system, you're running something fundamentally different from what you're deploying. This is doubly true for Javascript, where a common pattern is to store the image's node_volumes tree in a volume: so now your library tree is not what's in your image or what's on your local system, but a third machine-specific place that's hard to observe or update.)
